claims.evidence: NHS describes HRT as the main/primary medicine for menopause and perimenopause symptoms.

NICE text retrieved (2015 wording, current section 1.4 not seen) says offer HRT for vasomotor symptoms after discussing short- and longer-term benefits and risks; nothing states 'first'. 2024 update also puts menopause-specific CBT alongside HRT.
claims.newSentence: NICE advises offering HRT for hot flushes and night sweats after discussing the short- and long-term benefits and risks.

claims.evidence: CBT and lubricants/moisturisers for vaginal dryness are supported; 'certain medicines for hot flushes' not stated in retrieved text.
claims.newSentence: Options that do not use hormones include cognitive behavioural therapy and lubricants or moisturisers for vaginal dryness.

claims.evidence: NICE amended its unscheduled-bleeding recommendation (1.8.4/1.8.5) in 2026 but exact wording was not retrieved. NHS does state bleeding after 12 months without a period should be checked.
NICE NG23 covers vasomotor symptoms, genitourinary symptoms (vaginal oestrogen) and low mood/depressive symptoms in menopause.
Perimenopause as the transition before periods stop; NHS notes first sign is usually a change in periods.
NHS lists hot flushes, night sweats, poor sleep, low mood, anxiety, mood swings, brain fog, and change in period pattern.

Retrieved NHS list: headaches/migraines, joint and muscle pain, weight gain, skin changes, lower sex drive. Palpitations, incontinence, hair thinning not retrieved; 'weakening bones' is a long-term risk, not a symptom.
claims.newSentence: Others include headaches and migraines, joint and muscle pain, weight gain, skin changes and a lower sex drive.

claims.evidence: NHS: symptoms can have a big impact or you may hardly have any symptoms at all.
NHS: you reach menopause when you have not had a period for 12 months.

Age 45 to 55, may be earlier: supported (nhs.uk/conditions/menopause/). 'Perimenopause lasts a few months or several years' not stated; NHS symptoms page says symptoms usually last 7 to 9 years, sometimes longer.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says menopause usually affects people between the ages of 45 and 55, though it can happen earlier.

claims.evidence: NHS: HRT is the main medicine for menopause and perimenopause symptoms (duplicate of c01).
NHS HRT types: patches, gel, spray, implants (rarely used), tablets.
If you still have a womb, oestrogen must be taken with a progestogen so the womb lining does not thicken.
No retrieved text says a GP will discuss any risks.
NHS: hot flushes and night sweats often improve within a few weeks.
NHS: vaginal dryness and mood can take a few months; up to 3 months to work fully.
NHS: HRT can reduce risk of osteoporosis by raising oestrogen levels.
NHS: some HRT types slightly raise breast cancer risk; tablets carry a small increase in clot risk, patches/gels/sprays do not. Original omits that nuance.
claims.newSentence: Some types of HRT slightly raise the risk of breast cancer, and HRT tablets carry a small increase in the risk of blood clots.

claims.evidence: NHS: balance of benefits and risks depends on age, symptoms and risk factors; NICE advises discussing benefits and risks.
NHS: vaginal oestrogen as pessary, cream, gel or ring for vaginal dryness; NICE: offer vaginal oestrogen for genitourinary symptoms. 'Low-dose' and 'tablet' not stated.
claims.newSentence: Vaginal oestrogen, as a pessary, cream, gel or ring, can treat vaginal dryness and other genitourinary symptoms of the menopause.

claims.evidence: NHS says CBT can help with low mood and anxiety caused by menopause; sleep and physical symptoms, and 'certain medicines for hot flushes', not stated in retrieved text. NICE 2024: CBT for vasomotor symptoms where HRT is contraindicated or not wanted.
claims.newSentence: For people who cannot or choose not to take HRT, the NHS lists cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), which can help with low mood and anxiety caused by menopause and perimenopause.

claims.evidence: NHS: over-the-counter vaginal moisturisers or lubricants can be used.
NHS: regular exercise can reduce hot flushes; triggers to avoid include spicy food, caffeine, smoking, alcohol. 'Weight-bearing' not stated; wording is instruction-like.
claims.newSentence: The NHS suggests that regular exercise may reduce hot flushes, and that spicy food, caffeine, smoking and alcohol can be triggers.

claims.evidence: NHS: contact a GP to discuss options if you have symptoms; GP may suggest HRT if flushes are frequent or severe. 'Speak to a GP if frequent or severe' not stated as such.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says people with menopause or perimenopause symptoms can talk to a GP about their options.

claims.evidence: NICE referral criteria for non-response or side effects were not found in retrieved text.
Exact NICE unscheduled bleeding wording not retrieved (amended 2026, relates to bleeding on systemic HRT); duplicate of c04.
Bleeding after 12 months without a period needing GP check is supported. Palpitations and heavier bleeding advice not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: The NHS advises seeing a GP about any vaginal bleeding after periods have stopped for 12 months or more, even if it has only happened once.

claims.evidence: Search returned nothing on menopause before 40 or its causes.
Only a 2015 draft wording on HRT for low mood was seen; not confirmed in current 2024 guideline.
NHS lists low mood and poor sleep as symptoms; support lines are 24/7. Wording 'help is open' is awkward.
claims.newSentence: Menopause can affect mood and sleep. If low mood becomes severe or there are thoughts of self-harm, help is available at any time.

claims.evidence: Local NHS trust pages: if in immediate danger or physically harmed, call 999 or go to A&E.
NHS trust pages: NHS 111 option 2 for urgent mental health support, 24/7, for self or someone else.
GP practice NHS page: Samaritans listen any time, 116 123, free.

notes: Current NICE NG23 section wording (1.4 HRT, 1.8 bleeding, referral, low mood) was not retrieved verbatim; claims depending on it were edited or removed. Crisis-line sources (c32-c34) are local NHS trust/GP pages, not national; the 111 option 2 URL cites an English trust, the Samaritans URL a Welsh GP page, so suggest re-verifying against nhs.uk/nhs.uk mental-health pages and samaritans.org. No sentence called a medicine safe; the search summary used 'safe and effective' for HRT, which should not be echoed. 'Weakening bones' in c08 is a long-term risk not a symptom. Overlap: c01/c12 and c04/c27/c28 duplicate each other; consider merging.
